speaker: johnstewart
text: Good evening, everyone. Welcome to Beaumont's regular city council meeting of Tuesday, March 23rd. As always, we are pleased to be here today on the traditional territory of Treaty 6. We acknowledge all those who share a deep connection with this land. The city of Beaumont respects the histories, languages, and cultures of all of Canada's First Peoples, whether they be a First Nation, Métis, or Inuit descent, and appreciates that their presence continues to enrich Canada's vibrant communities. We are all Treaty people. Just before we get going with the agenda, we do have two proclamations tonight, and we're getting some feedback from somebody. So just a quick reminder, if you're not on, put yourself on mute, please. Two proclamations tonight. First one is National Safe Digging Month, April 2021. Whereas each year, the integrity of Alberta's underground infrastructure is jeopardized by damage during ground disturbance activities caused by those who fail to call or click before you dig. And whereas the consequences of damage to buried facilities can include service disruptions, environmental contamination, property damage, and personal injury, and even death. And whereas the Alberta Common Ground Alliance and its members promote the principles of damage prevention best practices, including the need to call or click before you dig. And whereas ground disturbers, including contractors, homeowners, and landowners, can save time and money and keep our province safe and connected by following damage prevention best practices, including making that simple call to Alberta OneCall. And whereas the stakeholders in the buried facility damage prevention process, the digging community, buried facility owners, operators, buried facility locators, regulatory agencies, training organizations, and the OneCall Center all agree that the prevention of damage to buried facilities is a shared responsibility. Now, therefore be it resolved that I, Mayor John Stewart, do hereby proclaim April 2021 is National Safe Digging Month in the city of Beaumont, Alberta, dated this 22nd day of March, 2021. And we also have the proclamation for Earth Hour on March 27th, 2021, from 8.30 p.m. to 9.30 p.m. Whereas our nation's use of energy continues to increase, resulting in detrimental effects on the world's climate. And whereas it has been estimated that turning non-essential lights out in Canada for one hour could save as much as 15% of the energy consumed on an average Saturday night. And whereas the energy savings will reduce carbon emissions into our air, preserve the natural resources used to produce this energy, set a positive precedent for the rest of the nation, and result in ongoing reduced costs for the community, taxpayers, and businesses of the city of Beaumont. And whereas participation in Earth Hour 2021 will provide the residents of the city of Beaumont with insight into the impact of lights on energy consumption and raise community awareness on the need to conserve energy whenever possible. Therefore be it resolved that I, Mayor John Stewart, hereby proclaim March 27th, 2021, from 8.30 p.m. to 9.30 p.m. as Earth Hour in the city of Beaumont, Alberta, dated the 23rd day of March, 2021. So pleased to do that today. Next up on the agenda is adoption of the agenda. Are there any changes to the agenda? Ms. Winter?

speaker: curtisdublanko
text: Thank you. Good evening to the mayor and council. Before you is a report regarding residential property tax rate applied to Fairland condos. In the later in 2020, in the fall, some condo associations have expressed concerns that their property owners are taxed inequitably in relation to the municipal services utilized. Administration research past council decisions to gain understanding of past and current treatment for the assessment class of condominiums and analyze any concerns presented by these associations. Past practice from 2002 to 2007, the then town of Oma did have a separate rate for these types of properties. This practice was subsequently reversed for the 20, sorry, 2008 tax year and beyond. Regarding municipal services, public versus private property, listed below on the report are a number of services condo associations have cited as examples of services that are paid for by condo residents as part of their condo fees. Specific ones being roadway and sidewalk maintenance, including snow clearing and street sweeping, utility servicing within the condo property, such as flushing, as well as street lighting costs, electricity. It is an important distinction to be aware of that the services noted are on privately owned property rather than municipal infrastructure. These services are only performed by the municipality on city owned assets and infrastructure and the city does not provide these service on any privately owned property. Providing services to private assets exposes the city to increased liability risk and obviously operating costs. Included in the report are some summaries of the individual service levels provided to the publicly owned infrastructure. I'm not going to go through every single one. Regarding assessment and taxation as a whole, property taxes help pay for municipal services, including fire, police, road maintenance, snow removal, parks and rec services to name a few. It's important to note that the specific amount of municipal services utilized by an individual taxpayer may vary greatly. A good examples are parks and trails. Some residents might use them greatly, others might not use them at all. Property taxes are a means of distributing the net cost of municipal services among all property owners based on their assessed property value rather than a fee for specific services. For this reason, the rationale that some of these condo associations utilize less city services might not necessarily be accurate. Summarize this a little more simply, a property owner's tax levy does not directly pay for the infrastructure adjacent to their property. Their levy is their pro rata contribution to the overall operations of the city. From a budget financial impact, introducing a separate residential assessment subclass for condos with a lower rate may result in a shift of the overall tax burden away from condo owners and onto other non-residential and residential property owners. As part of the 2021 budget deliberations, council approved a 0% tax levy. Also as part of these deliberations, the ratio of residential to non-residential property tax rates was discussed and coming shortly, admin will be bringing forth a taxation policy which will provide some further guidance and recommendations to council on the ratio. Thank you, I'm able to take any questions council may have.
